title: Logic families compared: TTL, CMOS; voltage levels and power

items.prompt: A TTL gate input is left unconnected. How does the gate read it?
options: As a 1 (high).
As a 0 (low).
As random noise.
The gate stops working.
items.explanation: A floating TTL input is pulled up internally and reads as high. The simulator on the bench shows a floating input as ?, which is kinder but not what real hardware does.

items.prompt: In standard 5 V TTL, what is the maximum voltage an input accepts as a **0** (V<sub>IL</sub>)?
items.explanation: TTL: V<sub>IL</sub> = 0.8 V, V<sub>IH</sub> = 2.0 V, V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.4 V, V<sub>OH</sub> = 2.4 V.

items.prompt: How are the input thresholds of a plain CMOS gate (such as 74HC) set?
options: They scale with the supply voltage, roughly 30% and 70% of V<sub>DD</sub>.
They are fixed at 0.8 V and 2.0 V whatever the supply.
They are always exactly 0 V and 5 V.
They are set by an external resistor.
items.explanation: At 5 V that is about 1.5 V and 3.5 V; at 3.3 V about 1.0 V and 2.3 V. This is why mixing families needs care.

items.prompt: A 3.3 V CMOS output (V<sub>OH</sub> ≈ 3.3 V) drives a 5 V TTL input. Will the TTL gate read a 1 reliably?
options: Yes: 3.3 V is above TTL's V<sub>IH</sub> of 2.0 V.
No: TTL needs at least 5 V to read a 1.
No: TTL inputs need a negative voltage for a 1.
Only if the wire is shorter than 1 cm.
items.explanation: TTL's thresholds are low, so a 3.3 V part drives it fine. The other direction is the problem.

items.prompt: A 5 V TTL output (V<sub>OH</sub> min 2.4 V) drives a 5 V plain CMOS input (V<sub>IH</sub> ≈ 3.5 V). What is the risk?
options: The CMOS gate may not read the high reliably: 2.4 V is in its forbidden zone. Use a pull-up resistor or an HCT part.
No risk: 2.4 V is a valid high for everything.
The CMOS gate will be destroyed by 2.4 V.
The TTL gate will be destroyed.
items.explanation: This is the classic TTL-to-CMOS interface problem. 74HCT parts have TTL-level inputs precisely to solve it.

items.prompt: Which of these are genuine advantages of CMOS over TTL?
options: Very low static power.
Works over a wide range of supply voltages.
Inputs draw almost no current, so fan-out is large at low speed.
Unconnected inputs are harmless.
items.explanation: Floating CMOS inputs are the opposite of harmless. Everything else on the list is true.

items.prompt: Why must unused CMOS inputs be tied to the supply or to ground?
options: A floating input can drift to mid-rail, turning on both transistors: the gate draws heavy current and its output flickers.
Otherwise the gate reads a permanent 1.
To make the chip easier to solder.
So the gate runs faster.
items.explanation: Mid-rail inputs defeat the whole point of complementary switching. A chip with floating inputs can get warm and behave randomly.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a **74HC** and a **74HCT** part?
options: HCT has TTL-compatible input thresholds, so TTL outputs can drive it; HC has CMOS thresholds that scale with the supply.
HCT is twice as fast as HC.
HC runs on 5 V only; HCT runs on 3.3 V only.
HCT parts have more inputs.
items.explanation: Both are CMOS inside. The T stands for TTL-compatible inputs.

items.prompt: A 74LS gate dissipates about 2 mW. A chip holding 4 such gates dissipates about how much, all the time?
items.explanation: TTL burns power even when idle: 4 × 2 mW = 8 mW. A CMOS 74HC00 at rest uses microwatts.

items.prompt: Which family's power consumption rises almost in proportion to switching frequency?
options: CMOS, because almost all its power is spent charging capacitance on each transition.
TTL, because its transistors saturate.
Both rise equally.
Neither: power does not depend on frequency.
items.explanation: At very high frequencies CMOS can use as much as TTL; at rest it uses almost nothing.
